Job seeker Eric Clardy, right, shakes hands with recruiter Raul Mendez from L.A. County Probation Department. And that was music to the ears of 30-year-old Eric Clardy. It has been a rough couple of years for Clardy. He was laid off from his job as a loan processor when the real estate market started to tank. Then, after finding work as a project manager for a plumbing company, layoffs struck again. "It's kind of like, get the job now so you can pay your bills, then start towards the career that you really want," he said. Clardy said his goal is to make contact with at least 10 potential employers a day via phone, letters and the Internet. Being unemployed is hard work, too.  Watch how Clardy goes about trying to find a job » . "It was a scramble," Clardy said. "I was selling insurance, doing temp jobs, going to job fairs." The city of Los Angeles and the California Employment Development Department organized Saturday's event, which they said drew about 10,000 people. Earlier this month, a two-day job fair to fill some 500 part-time jobs at the stadium during baseball season drew about 7,000 applicants. California's unemployment rate is 10.1 percent, a full 2 percentage points higher than the national rate. The state's Employment Development office estimates that nearly a half-million state residents have lost their jobs in the past year. "We are not seeing as many job opportunities as we saw a year ago," said Gloria Bratton Moore, who runs the state-funded Work Source job center in Los Angeles. Nonetheless, she said, "There are jobs available." But at Dodger Stadium, it was clear that competition for those available jobs is stiff. Applicants were often stacked four and five people deep in front of employer tables, and there was little chance for most of the 10,000 job seekers to make much of an impression. But organizers worked hard to pump up any flagging spirits. "Yes we can. Yes we can," Los Angeles School Board member Monica Garcia chanted over a loudspeaker. State lawmaker Kevin deLeon told the crowd that they are among the nation's hardest-hit in this economic downturn, but he exhorted them to not give up. "We will get out of this economic funk," he said. "We will recover soon. We've got to have hope." Garcia and deLeon's comments echoed the campaign slogans of President Obama, who recently won approval of a nearly $800 billion economic stimulus package. Recruiters from the government agencies present at the job fair said that money will start creating jobs within the next few months. The Army Corps of Engineers told applicants that it is hiring for a wide variety of positions, including those for engineers, heavy-equipment operators and environmental field workers. The Commerce Department is adding more than 1 million jobs in preparation of the 2010 census, and other federal agencies are hiring as well. All of that was good news to Clardy, who left resumes and filled out applications at a number of the 80 booths cluttering the stadium's parking lot. But he remained realistic about this day's activities leading directly to a job. "It seemed like a couple of years ago, the job fair was really your first interview," he said. "Now it doesn't seem like that. Some companies are not even taking resumes at the job fairs anymore."

After securing new employment as a project manager for a plumbing company, he was hit by layoffs once again. 

"It's kind of like, get the job now so you can pay your bills, then start towards the career that you really want," Clardy explained. 

Clardy makes it his daily goal to contact at least 10 potential employers via phone, mail, and the internet, proving that searching for work is a full-time endeavor in itself. "It was a scramble," he recalled of his recent efforts. "I was selling insurance, doing temp jobs, going to job fairs."

Organized jointly by the City of Los Angeles and the California Employment Development Department, Saturday's event drew an estimated 10,000 attendees. It follows a job fair held earlier this month that attracted roughly 7,000 applicants competing for just 500 part-time seasonal positions at the stadium. 

California’s economic landscape remains grim. The state's unemployment rate stands at 10.1 percent—a full two percentage points above the national average. Furthermore, the Employment Development Department estimates that nearly half a million Californians have lost their jobs over the past year. 

"We are not seeing as many job opportunities as we saw a year ago," noted Gloria Bratton Moore, director of the state-funded WorkSource job center in Los Angeles. Nonetheless, she added, "There are jobs available."

"It seemed like a couple of years ago, the job fair was really your first interview," Clardy observed. "Now it doesn't seem like that. Some companies are not even taking resumes at the job fairs anymore."

**Desperate for Opportunity: 10,000 Job Seekers Swarm Dodger Stadium as Los Angeles Tackles Economic Crisis**

**LOS ANGELES** — On a day usually reserved for baseball, the concourses of Dodger Stadium filled with a very different kind of crowd. Seeking a lifeline amidst a turbulent economy, an estimated 10,000 hopeful job seekers converged on Chavez Ravine for one of the largest career fairs in Southern California’s recent history. 

Jointly organized by the City of Los Angeles and state employment officials, the massive initiative was launched in direct response to severe job losses and rising unemployment rates that have hit the region hard. By transforming the iconic sports venue into a giant recruitment hub, organizers aimed to bridge the gap between struggling workers and employers eager to rebuild their workforces. 

The backdrop to the event is a grim economic reality. Over the past year, California has grappled with widespread layoffs across multiple sectors—ranging from tech and entertainment to logistics, retail, and hospitality. High inflation, shifting industry demands, and corporate downsizing have left thousands of residents without steady income, pushing local unemployment figures well above pre-crisis levels. 

By sunrise, hours before the gates were scheduled to open, lines of applicants wrapped around the stadium perimeter. The crowd was a cross-section of the city itself: recent college graduates looking for their first big break, mid-career professionals navigating unexpected layoffs, and older workers forced out of retirement by the rising cost of living. Cluttered with portfolios and stacks of freshly printed résumés, attendees stood shoulder-to-shoulder, reflecting the deep anxiety and urgency gripping the local labor market.

Inside, more than 80 hiring organizations set up shop along the stadium concourses. The participating employers represented a broad spectrum of industries, including public safety, transportation, healthcare, education, municipal government, and private enterprise. Major agencies such as Metro, the Los Angeles Police Department, and local hospital networks offered positions ranging from entry-level administrative roles to specialized technical positions. Several companies took advantage of the venue's scale to conduct preliminary, on-the-spot interviews and extend immediate conditional job offers.

For many attendees, the event provided a relief from the impersonal nature of digital job hunting. "Applying online often feels like shouting into a void—you send out hundreds of résumés and never hear a word back," said Marcus Vance, a laid-off logistics worker from East LA. "Being able to look a recruiter in the eye, hand them my résumé, and explain my experience in person makes a world of difference. It gives you your dignity back."

State and local officials acknowledged that while a single job fair cannot solve systemic economic woes, creating direct access to employment is a critical first step. 

"Our goal today was to meet people where they are and provide immediate, tangible solutions to families in crisis," said a spokesperson for the California Employment Development Department. "The massive turnout proves both the necessity of these events and the immense resilience of our workforce."

As the event wrapped up in the late afternoon, the massive crowd began to disperse, leaving behind a stadium floor cleared of booths but filled with tentative hope. While the turnout of 10,000 job seekers underscored the sheer scale of California's economic challenges, it also demonstrated an unyielding drive among its workers to move forward. For hundreds of attendees who walked away with follow-up interviews or job offers, Chavez Ravine wasn't just a ballpark—it was the place where their economic recovery finally began.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about a massive job fair at Dodger Stadium during the late 2000s recession, featuring a job seeker named Eric Clardy. Include realistic details like state unemployment stats, participating employers, and politician quotes.
counterfactuals.output:
**LOS ANGELES (CNN)** — On a searing Thursday morning, the parking lots of Dodger Stadium were packed to capacity. But there were no tailgaters, no foam fingers, and no smell of Dodger Dogs in the air. 

Instead, a line of more than 12,000 men and women in conservative business suits and polished dress shoes stretched past the center field gates, wrapping twice around Chavez Ravine. Carrying crisp stacks of résumés in plastic sleeves, they waited under a unforgiving sun for a chance at something that has become increasingly rare in Southern California: a job.

The event, billed as the "SoCal Regional Career Summit," is one of the largest job fairs in California since the onset of the Great Recession. It offered a stark, visual reminder of the economic wreckage sweeping across the nation's most populous state.

For 39-year-old Eric Clardy, the day began at 4:30 a.m. 

"I wanted to be first in line, but when I pulled up, there were already hundreds of headlights lined up at the gate," said Clardy, a former logistics coordinator from Torrance who was laid off eight months ago when his freight shipping company downsized. "You look around and you see people who used to be managers, engineers, accountants—all standing in the heat, desperate just to hand a paper application to a recruiter."

Clardy, wearing his only tailored suit, clutched a leather portfolio containing 50 copies of his résumé. "Eight months ago, I thought I’d be off the market in two weeks," Clardy said, adjusting his tie. "Today, I’m hoping to get five minutes with a manager from a warehouse firm just to earn half of what I used to make. You have to swallow your pride."

### A State in Crisis

The scene at Dodger Stadium comes as California grapples with an unprecedented employment crisis. According to the California Employment Development Department (EDD), the state’s unemployment rate surged to a staggering 11.5% this month—its highest level in more than seven decades. In Los Angeles County, the number is even grimmer, hovering near 12.3%, with an estimated 600,000 residents officially out of work.

Housing foreclosures, the collapse of the subprime mortgage market, and severe pullbacks in consumer spending have hammered the Golden State's economy, leaving local governments and private industries reeling.

"What we are seeing today at Chavez Ravine is not just a job fair; it is a mirror reflecting the deep economic pain of our working families," Los Angeles Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa said during a brief morning press conference near home plate. "The American Dream is being tested right here in Los Angeles. But by bringing public utilities, law enforcement, and private sector employers under one roof, we are sending a message that we will leave no stone unturned to get Angelenos back to work."

### Few Openings, Endless Lines

Despite the massive turnout, the reality inside the stadium was sobering. Organizers estimated that the 85 participating companies had roughly 1,500 open positions combined—meaning roughly eight job seekers were competing for every single opening.

With major corporate recruiters largely absent due to hiring freezes, the longest lines stretched toward government entities, healthcare providers, and low-wage retail operations that have managed to weather the downturn. 

Among the employers present were the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department, Kaiser Permanente, Target, and Home Depot. Military recruiters from the U.S. Army and Navy also reported overwhelming interest from applicants far older than their traditional high school target demographic.

"In my fifteen years in human resources, I have never seen talent of this caliber applying for entry-level positions," said Sarah Jenkins, a recruiter for a regional security firm hiring guard staff for $11 an hour. "We have people with master's degrees applying to work night-shift security. It's heartbreaking, but it speaks to the severity of this downturn."

### Searching for Hope

By noon, as temperatures hit the mid-80s, stadium personnel began distributing bottled water to the thousands still waiting outside the turnstiles. EDD representatives set up impromptu tables along the concourse to help overwhelmed attendees file for extended unemployment benefits on the spot.

For Clardy, after nearly five hours of waiting and navigating thronged concourses where concession stands normally sell peanuts and beer, he managed to drop off résumés with three companies. None could guarantee an interview.

Still, as he walked back to his car parked near the top deck of the stadium, Clardy tried to remain optimistic.

"You can't give up," Clardy said, looking down at the vast sea of job seekers still snaking through the parking lot below. "When you're sitting at home applying on the internet, you feel like you're the only one drowning. Out here today, you realize you're part of an army of people trying to survive. We just have to keep pushing until the tide turns."

**Desperation at Chavez Ravine: How a 2009 Job Fair at Dodger Stadium Defined LA’s Economic Crisis**

On a bright spring morning in April 2009, Chavez Ravine was flooded with thousands of visitors. But they hadn’t come to buy hot dogs, drink beer, or cheer on the Los Angeles Dodgers. 

Instead, a sea of men and women in dark business suits, tailored dresses, and polished dress shoes stood under the sweltering Southern California sun, clutching stacks of freshly printed resumes. They were there for the Los Angeles Diversity Job Fair—an event that would become one of the most poignant visual metaphors for the devastation of the Great Recession.

By the time the stadium gates opened, an estimated 10,000 job seekers had descended upon the ballpark, creating bumper-to-bumper traffic that backed up onto the 110 Freeway. For a city drowning in unemployment, Dodger Stadium had transformed from a temple of leisure into the epicenter of a historic economic struggle.

### The Anatomy of a Crisis

To understand the desperation at Dodger Stadium that day, one must look at the economic landscape of 2009. The collapse of the housing market and the subsequent global financial meltdown had hit California with brutal force. 

In early 2009, the unemployment rate in Los Angeles County was climbing toward a crushing 11%, on its way to a peak of over 12% a year later. Industries that had long fueled the local economy—construction, real estate, manufacturing, retail, and even segments of the entertainment industry—were hemorrhaging jobs. 

Every day brought news of layoffs, foreclosures, and corporate bankruptcies. For tens of thousands of Angelenos, savings accounts were dwindling, unemployment benefits were running out, and traditional job boards had yielded months of silence. 

When news spread that a massive job fair was being hosted at Dodger Stadium, promising access to dozens of employers, it ignited a desperate spark of hope.

### A Line Wrapped Around History

The scene at the stadium was striking, tragic, and surreal. 

Job seekers began arriving in the pre-dawn hours, hours before the event was scheduled to begin. By mid-morning, the queue stretched for miles, snaking around the stadium’s vast parking lots and winding along the concrete concourses where fans usually lined up for concessions. 

What made the crowd so remarkable was its sheer diversity. The Great Recession was an equal-opportunity destroyer, and the line at Dodger Stadium reflected that grim reality. 

Side-by-side in the heat stood 22-year-old recent college graduates who couldn’t find an entry-level foot in the door, mid-career professionals with decades of experience who had been laid off in corporate downsizings, and workers in their late 50s and 60s whose retirement funds had been wiped out by the Wall Street collapse. Former mortgage brokers rubbed shoulders with construction workers, graphic designers, and former middle managers.

Many had waited in line for three or four hours just to pass through the metal detectors and reach the concourse where the employer booths were set up.

### Cruel Arithmetic: The Supply and Demand Imbalance

Once inside, the harsh reality of the 2009 job market set in. While the turnout was overwhelming, the actual opportunities were agonizingly scarce. 

Roughly 50 to 60 employers had set up tables, ranging from law enforcement agencies and local government departments to security firms, insurance companies, and military recruiters. Few corporate titans or high-paying white-collar firms were hiring. 

The arithmetic was brutal: 10,000 desperate applicants competing for perhaps a few hundred concrete openings. At booth after booth, representatives were overwhelmed, quickly running out of informational flyers and resorting to telling candidates—who had spent hours in the heat—to simply "apply online."

Many candidates walked away from the stadium with bruised spirits, having traded hours of waiting for little more than a polite nod and a URL. 

### A Symbol of the Great Recession

Photos and television footage of the Dodger Stadium job fair made national and international news. Images of thousands of smartly dressed job seekers lining the stadium’s concourses became visual shorthand for the depth of the American economic disaster, inviting comparisons to the breadlines of the Great Depression.

It highlighted a profound shift in the American workforce. It showed that the crisis was no longer confined to subprime mortgage lenders or Wall Street bankers; it had bled into the everyday lives of ordinary citizens in major metropolitan areas. 

### Legacy of a Dark Era

Eventually, Los Angeles recovered. The economic engine restarted, unemployment rates fell, and Dodger Stadium returned to hosting ballgames, concerts, and celebrations.

Yet, for those who stood in the concrete heat of Chavez Ravine in April 2009, the day remains an indelible memory. It was a moment when the collective vulnerability of an entire city was laid bare, capturing a time when thousands of people, pushed to the brink by an unpredictable global crisis, put on their best clothes and lined up just for the chance to work.

By **Dan Simon**, CNN
July 16, 2009 | Updated 6:42 PM EDT

**(CNN) —** Before the morning sun had cleared the downtown skyline, the line outside the Los Angeles Convention Center had already wrapped around three city blocks. 

Men and women in pressed suits, sweat soaking through their collars in the 85-degree heat, clutched worn leather portfolios. Some had been waiting since 3:00 a.m. They weren't waiting for concert tickets or the latest smartphone. They were waiting for a shot at a paycheck.

California—once the engine of American economic growth—is now the epicenter of a national crisis. With the state’s unemployment rate hovering at a staggering 11.6%, a local diversity job fair on Tuesday drew an estimated 6,000 applicants for fewer than 300 available positions.

> **[WATCH: Thousands line up before sunrise at LA Convention Center as California unemployment hits record high]**

"What we are seeing today is unprecedented in modern California history," said Jack Kyser, chief economist for the Los Angeles County Economic Development Corporation. "It’s not just blue-collar workers who are hurting. It’s middle management, real estate professionals, architects, and teachers. The safety nets are tearing, and the state’s fiscal crisis is only compounding the panic."

---

### 'I just want to provide for my kids'

For 44-year-old Marcus Vance, standing near the back of the massive line, the economic collapse isn’t a matter of statistics—it’s a daily battle for survival. 

For twelve years, Vance worked as a senior project manager for a major residential homebuilder in the Inland Empire. But when the subprime mortgage bubble burst, the construction industry ground to a halt. Vance was laid off ten months ago. Since then, his savings have evaporated, his Moreno Valley home is deeply underwater, and his unemployment checks are running out.

```
[PHOTO: Job seeker Marcus Vance, 44, holds his resumes while waiting in a line of over 5,000 people outside the Los Angeles Convention Center on Tuesday. Photo: Mark Ralston/AFP via Getty Images]
```

"Two years ago, I was making six figures, managing a crew of fifty people, and planning for my kids' college funds," Vance said, adjusting his tie with trembling fingers. "Today, I'm here hoping to get an interview for a night-shift security guard or an entry-level retail associate. I’ve sent out over 400 resumes. I’ve had three callbacks."

Vance’s story is increasingly typical across Southern California, where the collapse of the housing market triggered a domino effect through banking, retail, and local government.

"You swallow your pride real fast when you see your bank account hit double digits," Vance added, his voice breaking. "I don't care about my old title anymore. I just want to work. I just want to keep a roof over my family's head."

> **[WATCH: 'I've sent 400 resumes' — Laid-off project manager describes job hunt nightmare]**

---

### A brutal numbers game

Inside the convention hall, the mood was tense. Recruiter booths for companies like TSA, Bank of America, and local law enforcement were swamped with applicants holding advanced degrees, competing for positions that paid a fraction of their previous salaries.

Local officials acknowledge that the sheer volume of displaced workers is overwhelming the regional economy. 

"The reality is that local businesses are in survival mode," Los Angeles City Council President Eric Garcetti told CNN in an interview on the floor of the event. "We are doing everything we can at the city level to create green-energy jobs and infrastructure projects, but the scale of this recession requires massive federal support. People are hurting, and they need relief now."

```
[PHOTO: Applicants hand their resumes to a recruiter at a Los Angeles job fair. Hundreds of people competed for a handful of lower-wage openings. Photo: Damian Dovarganes/AP]
```

Compounding the problem is California's ongoing budget crisis. Just last week, state lawmakers began issuing registered warrants—effectively "IOUs"—to vendors and tax refund recipients to preserve cash, further damaging consumer confidence in the state.

---

### No guarantees

By 2:00 p.m., many employers at the fair had already run out of physical application forms, directing desperate job seekers to apply online—a frustrating response for those who had waited hours just to speak to a human being.

Marcus Vance finally made it inside the hall after four hours in line. He managed to drop off three resumes—one for a hotel front-desk clerk, one for an auto-parts warehouse, and one for a municipal maintenance job.

Walking back out into the blistering Los Angeles heat, he carried a light stack of business cards, but no job offers. 

"You have to stay hopeful, because the alternative is giving up, and I can't afford to give up," Vance said, heading toward the Metro station to save on parking. "I'll go home, log onto the computer, and start applying again tonight."

***

*CNN’s Sarah Aarthun contributed to this report.*

**LOS ANGELES TIMES**

**Desperation Meets Hope in Downtown L.A. as Thousands Queue for Stimulus-Funded Jobs**

**By Sarah Lin**  
*May 14, 2009*

**LOS ANGELES —** By 4:00 a.m. Thursday, the line outside the Los Angeles Convention Center stretched nearly three-quarters of a mile, wrapping around Figueroa Street and spilling onto Venice Boulevard. Thousands of job seekers—dressed in suit jackets, ironed button-downs, and work boots—stood shoulder-to-shoulder in the damp morning mist, clutching stacks of freshly printed résumés.

For 42-year-old Marcus Vance, the long wait was a small price to pay for even a slim chance at employment. 

Two years ago, Vance was making $85,000 a year as a framing supervisor for a residential developer building tracts in the Inland Empire. When the subprime mortgage crisis triggered a catastrophic collapse in California’s housing market, the homebuilder went under. Vance lost his job, then his Toyota Tacoma, and eventually his home in Riverside. 

"I’ve filled out over 300 applications online since last fall," Vance said, adjusting his tie as the sun began to break through the haze. "I’ve applied for retail, warehouse work, driving—anything. You get nothing back. Not even a 'no thanks.' Today feels like the first time in six months there’s actually something to stand in line for."

The event—the Southern California Career and Stimulus Opportunity Expo—was billed as one of the region's largest hiring drives since the enactment of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (ARRA). The $787 billion federal stimulus package, signed into law earlier this year, has slowly begun trickling down to local government agencies tasked with rebuilding California's battered economy.

California’s unemployment rate hit a historic 11.2% in April, with Los Angeles County bearing a massive share of the pain. The collapse of the real estate bubble didn't just sink construction crews; it dragged down mortgage brokers, escrow officers, landscapers, architects, and municipal workers funded by property taxes.

Inside the convention hall, the mood was tense, charged with a mixture of anxiety and determination. Recruiters from federal, state, and city agencies found themselves overwhelmed by the sheer volume and high qualifications of the applicants.

The California Department of Transportation (Caltrans) was one of the most heavily besieged booths at the expo. Armed with millions in new federal infrastructure grants, Caltrans is looking to fill hundreds of civil engineering, highway maintenance, and equipment operation roles for long-delayed freeway repair projects along the I-5 and U.S. 101 corridors.

"We usually see a steady stream of applicants at these events," said Elena Rivera, a hiring coordinator for Caltrans District 7. "Today, we had to request extra security just to manage the line at our booth. We are seeing former vice presidents of construction firms applying for entry-level road maintenance positions. The talent pool is incredible, but the level of desperation is heartbreaking."

Nearby, the U.S. Census Bureau drew an equally massive crowd. The agency is embarking on one of the largest temporary hiring surges in modern history as it prepares for the 2010 national headcount, offering temporary field representative positions funded directly by stimulus dollars. While temporary, the positions offer a crucial lifeline for families attempting to forestall foreclosure.

Other agencies actively accepting applications included the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power (LADWP)—which is using federal funds to hire for green-grid updates and energy-efficiency programs—and the California Department of Parks and Recreation, which is funding deferred maintenance projects across state parks.

Despite the infusion of government funding, officials warn that public-sector hiring alone cannot instantly reverse the damage wrought by the housing crash. Event organizers estimated that over 12,000 people attended the one-day expo, competing for roughly 1,500 open positions.

For many, the math remains grim.

"It’s a drop in the bucket, but right now, a drop feels like an ocean," said Jennifer Torres, 31, a former loan processor from Glendale who had been laid off 14 months ago. She spent her morning applying for a clerk position with the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, which is overseeing stimulus-funded flood control work along the Los Angeles River.

As the convention center doors began to close late Thursday afternoon, thousands of applicants walked back out into the bright sunshine, their folders lighter, but their futures still deeply uncertain.

Vance, who managed to drop off résumés with Caltrans and the city's Bureau of Sanitation, paused on the sidewalk outside the arena to take off his dress shoes, rubbing his sore feet.

"I gave it my best shot," Vance said, looking back at the dispersing crowd. "Now I just go home, turn on the computer, and wait for the phone to ring."
